questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The parabola having its focus at $(3,2)$ and directrix along the y-axis has its vertex at
questions.solution: Vertex of the parabola is a point which lies on the axis of the parabola, which is a line $\perp$ to the directrix through the focus, i.e., $\mathrm{y}=$ 2 and equidistant from the focus and directrix $x=0$, so that the vertex is $\left(\frac{3}{2}, 2\right)$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A straight line parallel to the line $2 \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}+5=0$ is also a tangent to the curve $y^{2}=4 x+5$. Then the point of contact is
questions.solution:
Given curve is $y^{2}=4 x+5$ on differentiating, we get
$2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=4 \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{2}{y}$
Given line is $2 x-y+5=0\Rightarrow y=2 x+5$
slope of line is 2 . Therefore,
$\frac{2}{y}=2 \Rightarrow y=1$
put $\mathrm{y}=1$ in the equation of curve, we get
$\begin{array}{l}
1=4 x+5 \\
x=-1
\end{array}
Hence, point of contact is $(-1,1)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The normal at the point $\left(\mathrm{at}_{1}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{at}_{1}\right)$ on the parabola, cuts the parabola again at the point whose parameter is
questions.solution:
Let thenormal a ' $\mathrm{t}_{1}$ ' cuts the parabola again at the point ' $t_{2}$ ' the equation of the normal at $\left(a t_{1}^{2}, 2 a t_{1}\right)$ is $y+t_{1} x=2 a t_{1}+a t_{1}^{3}$
Since it passes through the point ' $\mathrm{t}_{2}$ ' i.e

\begin{array}{l}
\left(\mathrm{at}_{2}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{at}_{2}\right) \\
\therefore \quad 2 \mathrm{at}_{2}+\mathrm{at}_{1} \mathrm{t}_{2}^{2}=2 \mathrm{at}_{1}+\mathrm{at}_{1}^{3} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2 \mathrm{a}\left(\mathrm{t}_{1}-\mathrm{t}_{2}\right)+\mathrm{at}_{1}\left(\mathrm{t}_{1}^{2}-\mathrm{t}_{2}^{2}\right)=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2+\mathrm{t}_{1}\left(\mathrm{t}_{1}+\mathrm{t}_{2}\right)=0 \quad\left(\because \mathrm{t}_{1}-\mathrm{t}_{2} \neq 0\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2+\mathrm{t}_{1}^{2}+\mathrm{t}_{1} \mathrm{t}_{2}=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{t}_{1} \mathrm{t}_{2}=-\left(\mathrm{t}_{1}^{2}+2\right) \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_{2}=-\left(\mathrm{t}_{1}+\frac{2}{\mathrm{t}_{1}}\right)
\end{array}

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation $y^{2}+3=2(2 x+y)$ represents a parabola with the vertex at
questions.solution:
The given equation can be rewritten as $(\mathrm{y}-1)^{2}=4\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)$ which is a parabola with its vertex $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$ axis along the line $y=1$, hence axis parallel to $x$-axis.
Its focus is $\left(\frac{1}{2}+1,1\right)$, i.e., $\left(\frac{3}{2}, 1\right)$.

questions.q: If the parabola $y^{2}=4$ ax passes through the point $(1,-2)$, then the tangent at this point is
questions.solution:
Since the parabola $y^{2}=4 a x$ passes through the point $(1,-2)$,

\therefore(-2)^{2}=4 \mathrm{a}(1) \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=1

Equation of tangent to the parabola at $(1,-2)$ is
$\mathrm{yy}_{1}=2 \mathrm{a}\left(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{x}_{1}\right)$ or

y(-2)=2(1)(x+1) \text { or } x+y+1=0

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the tangent to the parabola \(y^2=6 x\) at the point whose ordinate is 6 , is
questions.solution:
Let \(x_1\) be the abscissa of the point whose ordinate is 6 .
Since the point \(\left(\mathrm{x}_1, 6\right)\) lies on \(\mathrm{y}^2=6 \mathrm{x}\),
\(\therefore 36=6 \mathrm{x}_1 \text { or } \mathrm{x}_1=6\)
\(\therefore\) The point is \((6,6)\)
Equation of tangent at \((6,6)\) is
\(\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{y} \cdot 6=2 \cdot \frac{3}{2}(\mathrm{x}+6) \quad\left(\because \mathrm{yy}_1=2 \mathrm{a}\left(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{x}_1\right)\right) \\
& \text { or } \mathrm{x}-2 \mathrm{y}+6=0
\end{aligned}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The normals at three points $P, Q$ and $\mathrm{R}$ of the parabola $y^{2}=4 a x$ meet at $(h, k)$. The centroid of the $\Delta P Q R$ lies on
questions.solution:
The sum of ordinates of feet of normals drawn from a point to the parabola, $\mathrm{y}^{2}=4 \mathrm{ax}$ is always zero.
Now, as normals at three points $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ of parabola $y^{2}=4 a x$ meet at $(h, k)$.
⇒ The normals from $(h, k)$ to $y^{2}=4 a x$ meet the parabola at $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}$ and $\mathrm{R}$.
$\Rightarrow y$-coordinate $y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}$ of these points and R will be zero.
$\Rightarrow \quad y$-coordinate of the centroid of $\Delta P Q R$
i. e., $\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3}=\frac{0}{3}=0\therefore \quad$ centroid lies on $\mathrm{y}=0$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}\left(\frac{1-\mathrm{x}}{1+\mathrm{x}^{2}}\right)^{2} \mathrm{~d} \mathrm{x}$ is
questions.solution: Let $I=\int e^{x} \frac{(1-x)^{2}}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}} d x\Rightarrow I=\int e^{x} \frac{1+x^{2}-2 x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}} d x\quad=\int e^{x}\left[\frac{1+x^{2}}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}}-\frac{2 x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}}\right] d x\Rightarrow I=\int e^{x} \frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)} d x-2 \int e^{x} \cdot \frac{x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}} d x\Rightarrow I=\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)} \cdot e^{x}-\int e^{x} \cdot\left[-\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{-2}\right] 2 x d x\quad-2 \int \frac{e^{x} x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}} d x\Rightarrow I=\frac{e^{x}}{1+x^{2}}+2 \int \frac{e^{x} x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}} d x  -2\int\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{x}}{\left(1+\mathrm{x}^{2}\right)^{2}} \mathrm{dx}\Rightarrow I=\frac{e^{x}}{1+x^{2}}+C$

questions.q: The particular integral of $\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2} \mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{dx}^{2}}+2 \mathrm{y}=\mathrm{x}^{2}$ is
questions.solution:
If $\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+2 y=x^{2}\Rightarrow\left(D^{2}+2\right) y=x^{2} \quad\left[D \equiv \frac{d}{d x}\right]$
Particular integral $($ P.I. $)=\frac{1}{\mathrm{D}^{2}+2} \cdot \mathrm{x}^{2}=\frac{1}{2\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{D}^{2}}{2}\right)} \cdot \mathrm{x}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{D}^{2}}{2}\right)^{-1} \cdot\left(\mathrm{x}^{2}\right)\because(1+\mathrm{D})^{-1}=1-\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{D}^{2}-\mathrm{D}^{3}+\ldots \ldots\therefore$ P.I $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left[1-\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}^{2}}{2}\right)^{2}-\ldots .\right]\left(\mathrm{x}^{2}\right)\Rightarrow$ P.I. $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left[\mathrm{x}^{2}-\frac{\mathrm{D}^{2}}{2}\left(\mathrm{x}^{2}\right)\right]\Rightarrow$ P.I. $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left[\mathrm{x}^{2}-1\right]$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The condition that the line $\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{q}=1$ be a normal to the parabola $y^{2}=4 a x$ is]
questions.solution:
The line $\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{q}=1$ will be a normal to the parabola $y^{2}=4 a x$ if, for some value of $m$, it is identical with
$y=m x-2 a m-a m^{3} \quad$ i.e. $m x-y=(2 a m+\left.\mathrm{am}^{3}\right)$
Comparing coefficients, we get

\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{m}}{1 / \mathrm{p}}=\frac{-1}{1 / \mathrm{q}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{am}+\mathrm{am}^{3}}{1} \Rightarrow \mathrm{mp}=-\mathrm{q}, \quad \therefore \\
\mathrm{m}=-\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{p}} \text { and } \mathrm{mp}=\mathrm{m}\left(2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{am}^{2}\right)
\end{array}

or $\quad P=2 a+a m^{2}=2 a+a\left(\frac{-q}{p}\right)^{2}$
or $\quad \mathrm{p}=2 \mathrm{a}+\frac{\mathrm{aq}^{2}}{\mathrm{p}^{2}}$
or $\mathrm{p}^{3}=2 \mathrm{ap}^{2}+\mathrm{aq}^{2}$,
Which is the required condition.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The focus of the curve $y^{2}+4 x-6 y+13=0$ is
questions.solution:
The given equation of curve is:

y^{2}+4 x-6 y+13=0

which can be written as: $\mathrm{y}^{2}-6 \mathrm{y}+9+4 \mathrm{x}$
\begin{array}{l}
+4=0 \\
\Rightarrow\left(y^{2}-6 y+9\right)=-4(x+1) \\
\Rightarrow(y-3)^{2}=-4(x+1)
\end{array}

Put $Y=y-3$ and $X=x+1$
On comparing $Y^{2}=4 a X$
Length of focus from vertex, $a=-1$
At focus $X=a$ and $Y=0 \Rightarrow x+1=-1$
\begin{array}{l}
\Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=-2 \\
\therefore \mathrm{y}-3=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{y}=3 \\
\therefore \quad \text { Focus is }(-2,3)
\end{array}

questions.q: The normal at the point $\left(a t_{1}^{2}, 2 a t_{1}\right)$ on the parabola meets the parabola again in the point $\left(a t_{2}^{2}, 2 a t_{2}\right)$, then
questions.solution:
Equation of the normal at point $\left(\mathrm{at}_{1}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{at}_{1}\right)$ on parabola is
$\mathrm{y}=-\mathrm{t}_{1} \mathrm{x}+2 \mathrm{at}_{1}+\mathrm{at}_{1}^{3}$
It also passes through $\left(\mathrm{at}_{2}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{at}_{2}\right)\begin{aligned}
& \text { So, } \quad 2 \mathrm{at}_{2}=-\mathrm{t}_{1}\left(\mathrm{at}_{2}^{2}\right)+2 \mathrm{at}_{1}+\mathrm{at}_{1}^{3} \\
\Rightarrow & 2 \mathrm{t}_{2}-2 \mathrm{t}_{1}=-\mathrm{t}_{1}\left(\mathrm{t}_{2}^{2}-\mathrm{t}_{1}^{2}\right) \\
\Rightarrow & \mathrm{t}_{1}+\mathrm{t}_{2}=\frac{-2}{\mathrm{t}_{1}} \\
\Rightarrow & \mathrm{t}_{2}=-\mathrm{t}_{1}-\frac{2}{\mathrm{t}_{1}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The tangent lines to the curve $y^{2}=4 a x$ at points where $x=a$, are
questions.solution:
The given equation of the curve is $y^{2}=4 a x$
Differentiating both sides of $(1)$ with respect to $\mathrm{x}$, we get

2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=4 a ; \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{4 a}{2 y}=\frac{2 a}{y}

If $\psi$ be the angle which the tangent to the curve at ( $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})$ makes with the positive direction of $x$-axis then $\tan \psi=\frac{d y}{d x}$ or

\tan \psi=\frac{2 \mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{y}} \quad \ldots .(3), \quad[\mathrm{using}(2)]

At $x=a$, then from $(1), y^{2}=4 a \cdot a=4 a^{2} \Rightarrow y=\pm 2 \mathrm{a}$

Hence, we get two points $(\mathrm{a}, 2 \mathrm{a})$ and $(\mathrm{a},-$ 2a) on the curve.
$\mathrm{At}(\mathrm{a}, 2 \mathrm{a}) \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y}=2 \mathrm{a}$ and let $\psi=\psi_{1}$
\begin{array}{r}
\therefore \text { from (3) } \tan \psi_{1}=\frac{2 a}{2 a}=1=\tan 45^{\circ} \\
\Rightarrow \psi_{1}=45^{\circ} .
\end{array}

$\mathrm{At}(\mathrm{a},-2 \mathrm{a}), \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y}=-2 \mathrm{a}$ and let $\psi=\psi_{2}\therefore$ from (3), $\tan \psi_{2}=\frac{2 a}{-2 a}=-1=\tan 135^{\circ}$;
or $\psi_{2}=135^{\circ}$.
Hence the required angle between tangents to $(1) \operatorname{at}(\mathrm{a}, 2 \mathrm{a})$ and $(\mathrm{a},-2 \mathrm{a})=\psi_{2}-\psi_{1}=135^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=90^{\circ} .$
This shows that the tangent lines to (1) at $(a, 2 a)$ and $(a,-2 a)$ are perpendicular to each other.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If a chord which is normal to the parabola at one end and subtends a right angle at the vertex, then slope of the chord is
questions.solution:
Chord PQ is normal to the parabola at \(\mathrm{Q}\) and is equation is \(y=m x-2 a m-a m^3\) ...(1)
The slope of normal PQ is \(m=\tan \theta\). The joint equation of \(O P\) and \(O Q\) is obtained by making the equation of parabola \(y^2=4 a x\) homogeneous with the help of (1). Thus joint equation of lines \(\mathrm{OP}, \mathrm{OQ}\) is \(y^2=4 a x\left\{\frac{m x-y}{2 a m+a^3}\right\}\) or \(\mathrm{m}\left(2+\mathrm{m}^2\right) \mathrm{y}^2+4 \mathrm{xy}-4 \mathrm{mx}^2=0\) ...(2) Since \(\angle \mathrm{POQ}=\frac{\pi}{2}\), the sum of the coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) in (2) must be zero. \(\mathrm{m}\left(2+\mathrm{m}^2\right)-4 \mathrm{~m}=0 \text { or } \mathrm{m}\left(\mathrm{m}^2-2\right)=0\) As \(\mathrm{m} \neq 0\), we get \(\mathrm{m}^2=2\) or \(\mathrm{m}= \pm \sqrt{2}\). Thus, \(\mathrm{m}\) \(=\sqrt{2}\).

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $z$ satisfies the equation $|z|-z=1+2 i$, then $z$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given : $|z|-z=1+2 i$
If $z=x+i y$, then th is equation reduces to

\begin{array}{l}
|x+i y|-(x+i y)=1+2 i \\
\Rightarrow\left(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}-x\right)+(-i y)=1+2 i
\end{array}

On comparing real and imaginary parts of both sides of this equation, we get

\begin{array}{l}
\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}-x=1 \\
\Rightarrow \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}=1+x \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=(1+x)^{2} \\
\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=1+x^{2}+2 x \\
\Rightarrow y^{2}=1+2 x...(i) \\
\text { and }-y=2 \\
\Rightarrow y=-2
\end{array}

Putting this value in eq. (i), we get

\begin{array}{l}
(-2)^{2}=1+2 x \\
\Rightarrow 2 x=3 \Rightarrow x=\frac{3}{2} \\
\therefore z=x+i y=\frac{3}{2}-2 i
\end{array}
